newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya bank results disappoint, seen hitting bourse.
newsitem.headline: Kenya bank results disappoint, seen hitting bourse.

text.p: Barclays Bank of Kenya and Standard Chartered Bank on Friday announced marginal gains in 1996 profits which investment analysts described as disappointing.
Barclays posted a 2.477 billion-shilling ($45.1 million) profit after tax for the year ended 31 December, 1996 from 2.120 billion shillings in the previous year.
Barclays said it would give a dividend of seven shillings per share for a total dividend of 10 shillings or 100 percent.
Standard posted a 1.149 billion shillings profit after tax compared to 1.129 billion shillings last year. It gave a final dividend of 1.75 for a total dividend of 3.0.
"Neither of the banks registered a significant improvement. All they did was maintain last year's position," a broker said.
"If anything they appear tighter on their advances to shareholders," the broker added.
Barclays results came after the Nairobi Stock Exchange had closed on Friday and after its share had eased 3.0 to 114.
Standard, which announced results late on Thursday, eased to 51 from 60.
The NSE 20-share index shed 40.49 points to 3,473.99.

Brokers said the banks performed well below speculated earnings -- "We all thought Barclays would hit the 4-billion mark, considering they made an extra-ordinary profit from the sale of National Industrial Credit ," a broker said.
"Standard Chartered should at least have hit 2-billion," another broker added without giving any details.
Barclays, Standard, Kenya Commercial Bank and National Bank of Kenya are Kenya's leading banks.
Brokers said the market, which was on a bullish streak, would experience an immediate correction now that the results of leading financials had started streaming in.

"Our market is bonus driven. Already the announcement by Standard Chartered Bank had a negative impact on the share," a broker said. "Investors got a rude shock because many of them were buying the share anticipating a bonus issue," he added.

A Standard Chartered Bank statement blamed a depressed economy, severely competitive market environment and massive investment in a restructuring programme designed to improve customer service for the marginal gains.

A financial analyst said Kenya's current economy position had no direct bearing on the banks' results. He added that the central bank's decision to enforce strict policy on loan portfolio may be the cause of the lower-than-expected results.
Commercial banks now have to account for non-performing loans in their year statements and auditors are under strict instructions from the central bank to ensure this is done.
